newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich pledges to find common ground with Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich pledges to find common ground with Clinton.

text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, announcing "a truly historic moment" in American politics, pledged on Wednesday to work towards finding common ground with President Bill Clinton during the next Congress.

The Georgia Republican waited until 2:45 a.m. EST to declare his party's majority in the House of Representatives safe from Democratic encroachment and then said he hoped to make progress with Clinton on balancing the budget and stopping illegal drug use.

"There's no reason why we can't find a common ground on which to work together. Much of what he campaigned on was Republican policy," a tired but obviously relieved Gingrich told an audience consisting of two dozen die-hard supporters and several sleeping children.
"We ought to work with him, give him a chance to lead in the direction he campaigned on ... if he actually meant all of those nice things, it's going to be a very productive year."
The Republicans retained control of the Senate and the House, putting Clinton on the defensive at the start of his second term.

Gingrich's almost conciliatory tone was in sharp contrast with his firebrand rhetoric of last winter, when a budget standoff between the Republican-controlled Congress and the White House shut the government down twice.
At that time, Republicans had a 235-197 seat majority in the House.

Gingrich, who was blamed for the government shutdown, later became the Democrats' poster boy for unpopular Republican policies including Medicare in a national campaign to win back control of the congressional chamber.
On Wednesday, Gingrich said election results indicated the new Republican majority would shrink by five to 10 seats, thanks to the defeat of House freshmen.
"Some absolutely first-rate people went down to defeat," he observed.
But the 53-year-old speaker also sought to salvage a public endorsement for Republican legislative aims from Tuesday's vote.
"This is literally the first time in 68 years that we have been able to win a majority in the U.S. House back-to-back," he said.
"There's a desire by the country for common-sense change towards a smaller government and decentralizing power out of Washington and lower taxes.

"It is a wonderful tribute, first of all, to the American people, that despite millions and millions and millions of dollars of advertising, that they could look beyond the various statements and they could see what was involved and they could make decisions on their own," Gingrich added.
